query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling from the high‐temperature BCC state, differential elemental diffusion leads to localized segregation that creates elastic lattice strains, which then trigger the nucleation of secondary phases via a sluggish diffusion effect inherent to multicomponent alloys, thereby lowering the free energy of the system.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase, supersaturated BCC solid solution with minimal initial segregation.
generation.intervention: Prepare samples that are cooled under controlled rates (e.g., rapid quenching versus moderate cooling) and then expose them to a fixed annealing treatment at an appropriately elevated temperature for an equivalent duration. Optionally, a set of specimens may be pre-deformed to introduce additional defects that could enhance segregation kinetics.
generation.conditions: The mechanism is expected to operate when cooling rates allow sufficient atomic mobility for differential diffusion but are not so slow as to reach full equilibrium homogenization; it should not dominate under extreme rapid quenching (which freezes the uniform BCC state) or at temperatures where complete homogenization occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional gradients and the accompanying elastic lattice strains generated by elemental segregation serve as the mediators that promote nucleation of secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: As the alloy cools from the high-temperature BCC state, elements with different diffusivities and atomic sizes segregate unevenly, producing local variations in lattice parameters and building up elastic stresses. Once these stresses reach a critical level, they induce a transformation that results in the precipitation of secondary, more stable phases (such as σ or B2) while being modulated by the sluggish diffusion characteristic of multicomponent alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to rapidly quenched samples that remain largely homogeneous in the BCC state, samples cooled moderately (or pre-deformed to increase defect density) will show an increased fraction of secondary phases as evidenced by XRD peak splitting or new reflections, increased hardness due to interphase boundaries, and microstructural features (e.g., precipitates) identifiable by electron microscopy.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples that retain the uniform high-temperature BCC phase with negligible elemental segregation and low elastic strain.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should not apply when cooling is too fast to allow any segregation (thus preserving the single-phase BCC microstructure) or when the temperature is sufficiently high and held long enough to completely homogenize the elemental distribution, erasing the elastic strain gradients.
generation.uncertainty: The precise identity, volume fraction, and morphology of the secondary phases may depend sensitively on subtle variations in processing conditions and the relative diffusion rates of the elements; additionally, quantification of the stress threshold triggering the transformation is still uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 specimens: one set rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state and one set cooled at a moderate rate. Subject both sets to an identical low-temperature annealing step (e.g., 600 °C for 1 hour). Use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy to analyze phase composition and microstructure, and perform microhardness testing. Additionally, for a sub-set, pre-deform some samples prior to annealing to see if defect-enhanced segregation accelerates phase transformation.
measurements: XRD peak profiles (peak splitting or emergence of new reflections indicative of secondary phases)
Electron microscopy images showing precipitate morphology and elemental partitioning (using EDS or APT)
Microhardness values to detect strengthening associated with new interphase boundaries
Quantitative measurements of lattice strain or elastic stress (if available)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the moderately cooled (or pre-deformed) samples do not show any significant increase in the fraction of secondary phases, elastic strain indicators, or hardness relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, or if phase formation appears independent of the cooling rate and defect density, then the hypothesis that differential segregation-induced elastic strains drive the phase transformation would be falsified.

A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Microstructure and phase composition of L-PBF sample are very similar to those of the powder. The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable.
